Thus, even if ships sail with full sails, they nevertheless seem to stand still. Someone will eventually demonstrate in which parts of the heavens comets wander, why they travel so far removed from the others, and how large and of what kind they are. We are content with what has been discovered; let our descendants also contribute something to the truth. "We do not see through the stars to what is beyond," he says, "but we transmit our sight through comets." First, if that happens, it does not happen in that part where the star itself consists of thick and solid fire, but where a thin splendor runs out and disperses into a mane <note>Seneca refers to the comet's tail, often called a head of hair in antiquity</note>. You see through the gaps between the fires, not through the fires themselves. "All stars," he says, "are round; comets are elongated, from which it appears they are not stars." For who will concede to you that comets are long, when their nature, like that of the others, is actually a globe? However, their brightness is extended, just as the sun sends its rays far and wide. Yet the sun itself has one shape, and the light flowing from it has another. Thus the body of comets itself is rounded, but their splendor appears longer than that of other celestial bodies. "Why?" you ask. Tell me first why the moon receives a light so unlike the sun's, since it receives it from the sun? Why is it sometimes red, sometimes pale? Why does it have a livid and black color when it is excluded from the sight of the sun? Tell me why all the stars have a face somewhat unlike one another, and most different from the sun. Just as nothing prevents them from being celestial bodies even if they are not similar, so nothing prevents comets from being eternal and of the same lot as the rest, even if they do not have a similar face to them. Furthermore, what of the world itself? If you consider it, is it not composed of diverse things? Why is it that the sun always burns in Leo <note>The zodiac sign of the Lion</note> and scorches the earth with heat, but in Aquarius <note>The Water-Bearer</note> it tightens the winter and closes the rivers with frost? Yet both this star and that are of the same condition, though they are dissimilar in effect and nature. Within a very short time Aries <note>The Ram</note> <margin>† rises</margin> rises, while Libra <note>The Scales</note> sinks most slowly; and yet this star and that are of the same nature, though the former ascends in a brief time and the latter is drawn out for a long time. Do you not see how contrary the elements are to each other? There are heavy and light things, cold and hot, moist and dry. The entire harmony of this world consists of discord. You deny that a comet is a star because its shape does not correspond to the pattern, nor is it similar to the others. For you see, that star which returns to its place in the thirtieth year <note>The planet Saturn</note> is very similar to this one which revisits its seat within a year. Nature does not present its work according to a single form, but prides itself on variety itself. It made some things slower, others swifter than the rest. Some it made stronger, others more temperate; some it led out from the crowd so they might proceed individually and conspicuously, others it sent into a herd. He is ignorant of nature's power who does not think it is permitted to do anything except what it does more often. It does not show comets frequently; it assigned them a different place, different times, and motions unlike the others. It wished to honor the greatness of its work through these things, whose appearance is too beautiful for you to think them accidental, whether you consider their size or their brightness, which is greater and more burning than the rest. Their appearance truly has something distinguished and singular, not cast into a narrow space and cramped, but let down more freely and embracing the region of many stars. Aristotle says comets signify storms and the intemperance of winds and rains. What then? Do you not judge that to be a celestial body which announces future things? For this is not a sign of a storm in the way that oil sparking and the growth of rotten fungi are signs of future rain, or the way it is an indication of a raging sea if sea-coots <note>term: Fulicæ; possibly gulls or similar water birds</note> play on dry land, and leave their familiar marshes, and the heron flies above the high cloud. But it is so in the way that the equinox signifies the turning of the year into heat or cold, or the way those things which the <term>Chaldæi</term> <gloss>Chaldeans/astrologers</gloss> sing determine what is sad or joyful for those being born. So you may know this is so, the rising of a comet does not immediately threaten winds and rains, as Aristotle says, but <margin>The rising of a comet makes the whole year suspect.</margin> it makes the whole year suspect. From which it appears that it did not draw signs from its immediate surroundings to give signs for the immediate future, but has them stored up and compressed by the laws of the world. That comet which appeared in the consulship of Patruculus and Vopiscus brought about the things predicted by Aristotle and Theophrastus. For there were great and continuous storms everywhere; but in Achaia and Macedonia, cities were overthrown by earthquakes. "Their slowness," he says, "is proof that they are heavier and have much of the earthly in them." Furthermore, their very courses, for they are generally driven toward the poles. Both are false. I will speak of the former first: that those things which are moved more slowly are heavy. What then? Is the star of Saturn, which performs its journey most slowly of all, heavy? <summary>Seneca argues that comets are permanent celestial bodies despite their varied shapes and irregular appearances, asserting that nature's harmony is built on diversity and that comets serve as long-term omens rather than immediate weather signs.</summary>
